title: Spatially informed policies can accelerate green hydrogen demand - Nature Energy
gist: A short policy briefing arguing that EU green hydrogen instruments are almost entirely supply-side and ignore demand-side spatial spillovers, where adoption by one industrial user makes nearby adoption more likely. It prescribes four concrete fixes — stricter offtaker commitments in Hydrogen Valley calls, a spillover score in European Hydrogen Bank auctions, spillover-sequenced REPowerEU corridors, and prioritizing the Rhine–Ruhr and North Sea coast plus iron, steel and chemicals — backed by simulations over 14,108 prospective offtakers showing 37–41% better policy cost-effectiveness.

themes.theme: The demand-side blind spot in EU hydrogen policy

insights.claim: Aside from sectoral mandates for aviation, shipping and industrial hydrogen, EU hydrogen policy instruments remain primarily supply-side and do not account for demand-side interdependencies.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The diagnosis reframes Europe's hydrogen stall as a demand-design failure rather than a funding shortfall, which changes what the next policy cycle should buy.
insights.quote: aside from sectoral mandates for the aviation, shipping and industrial hydrogen sectors, EU policy instruments remain primarily supply-side

insights.claim: EU Hydrogen Valleys, though designed as a place-based policy enabling regional ecosystems, give limited consideration to demand: existing valleys target only 0.2 Mt of demand, about 1% of the EU's 2030 goal.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The EU's signature regional hydrogen programme is two orders of magnitude too small on the demand side to move the 2030 target.
insights.quote: existing valleys target 0.2 Mt demand or 1% of the EU’s 2030 goal

insights.claim: Less than 1% of EU hydrogen currently originates from green sources and only 7% of announced capacity has been completed on schedule.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Announced project pipelines are a badly unreliable indicator of realized green hydrogen supply, with a roughly 14-fold attrition rate on schedule.
insights.quote: less than 1% of EU hydrogen originates from green sources and only 7% of announced capacity has been completed on schedule

insights.claim: Amid demand uncertainties, the 2025 European Hydrogen Bank auction awarded only 23% of its €1.2 billion budget, evidence that current instruments are falling short of expectations.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: More than three-quarters of an allocated hydrogen subsidy budget went unspent, so capital availability is not what is throttling European hydrogen.
insights.quote: the 2025 European Hydrogen Bank auction awarded only 23% of its €1.2 billion budget

themes.theme: Spatial spillovers and where they concentrate

insights.claim: Green hydrogen uptake is shaped by spatial spillovers in which one user's adoption makes others in the same area more likely to follow, arising from shared infrastructure, supply chains and knowledge exchange.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Adoption is a network phenomenon rather than a series of independent plant-level decisions, which means subsidy design should account for who influences whom.
insights.quote: when one user adopts, others in the area are more likely to follow

insights.claim: The effect of spatial spillovers grows to more than twenty times its average when cost competitiveness is still low.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The neighbourhood effect is strongest exactly during the expensive early phase, so clustering support geographically pays off most while hydrogen is uneconomic.
insights.quote: The effect of these spillovers grows to more than twenty times their average when cost competitiveness is still low.

insights.claim: Spillover potential is highly concentrated in the industrial areas of Western–Central Europe, specifically the Rhine–Ruhr and North Sea coast, and in hard-to-abate sectors such as iron and steel and chemicals.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: It narrows the field to a small named set of regions and sectors where hydrogen infrastructure and offtake investment has the best chance of compounding.
insights.quote: Spillover potential is highly concentrated in industrial areas of Western–Central Europe (Rhine–Ruhr, North Sea coast) and hard-to-abate industrial sectors (iron and steel, chemicals)

insights.claim: Areas with high spillover potential overlap only partly with the hydrogen valleys the EU has designated and the import corridors defined by the European Hydrogen Backbone.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Existing designations were not drawn where demand would self-reinforce, implying a measurable misallocation in current place-based hydrogen spending.
insights.quote: Areas with high spillover potential are concentrated in industrial regions but overlap only partly with existing valleys and corridors.

insights.claim: In regional detail for North Rhine-Westphalia and Eastern Austria/Moravia, the highest-scoring prospective offtaker clusters are dominated by hard-to-abate industries.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The concentration holds at local as well as continental scale, so site-level screening rather than country-level allocation is the right unit for policy.
insights.quote: High-potential clusters are dominated by hard-to-abate industries.

insights.claim: A spatially informed demand-side intervention targeting spillover potential cuts policy cost per kilogram of additional green hydrogen demand by 37–41% (€0.83–0.96) versus a spatially neutral baseline, holding size, sector and cost competitiveness constant.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Redirecting the same subsidy to network-central sites buys close to 40% more demand per euro without increasing the budget.
insights.quote: reduces policy costs per kilogram of additional green hydrogen demand by 37–41% (€0.83–0.96) relative to a spatially-neutral baseline

insights.claim: The advantage persists in a realistic policy setting: adding a 10% spatial criterion to a European Hydrogen Bank-style auction still improves cost-effectiveness by 13–15%.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The gain does not require rebuilding the auction, only a modest re-weighting of the award rule, which makes adoption politically plausible.
insights.quote: adding a 10% spatial criterion to a European Hydrogen Bank-style auction still improves cost-effectiveness by 13–15%

insights.claim: The same spatial-targeting logic may extend to other technologies with value chain interdependencies, such as carbon capture.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: If it generalizes, spillover scoring becomes a reusable screening tool across the whole decarbonization subsidy stack, not just hydrogen.
insights.quote: Results may extend to other technologies with value chain interdependencies (such as carbon capture).

insights.claim: Revising EU Hydrogen Valley calls to require commitments from multiple large-scale offtakers could catalyse regional uptake.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: A single eligibility clause — multiple committed anchor offtakers — would convert an ecosystem grant programme into a demand-creation instrument.
insights.quote: Revising EU Hydrogen Valley calls to require commitments from multiple large-scale offtakers could catalyse regional uptake.

insights.claim: Adding demand or spatial spillover scores to European Hydrogen Bank auctions, or screening projects for strong demand linkages, could improve both cost-effectiveness and bid-to-contract conversion rates.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Conversion of awards into built projects, not the headline strike price, is identified as the metric the auction should optimize.
insights.quote: Adding demand or spatial spillover scores to European Hydrogen Bank auctions, or screening projects for strong demand linkages, could improve cost-effectiveness and bid-to-contract conversion rates.

insights.claim: REPowerEU hydrogen corridor investments should be sequenced to prioritize links between multiple industrial offtakers and regions with strong spillover potential.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Build order for hydrogen transmission is treated as a policy lever in its own right, with demand-linked segments first to avoid underused pipe.
insights.quote: REPowerEU hydrogen corridor investments should be sequenced to prioritize links between multiple industrial offtakers and regions with strong spillover potential.

insights.claim: The study pairs an installation-level model of green hydrogen demand diffusion, calibrated on natural gas power generation as a historical analogue, with an original harmonized geospatial dataset of 14,108 prospective offtakers across industry, transport, power and heating, simulating adoption from 2024 to 2100.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The findings are conditional on hydrogen diffusing like natural gas power generation, and the underlying asset database is a reusable map of Europe's fossil-to-hydrogen switching candidates.
insights.quote: combines an installation-level model of green hydrogen demand diffusion (calibrated on natural gas power generation as a historical analogue) with an original dataset

insights.claim: Spillover potential is quantified using network centrality measures that capture connectivity between offtakers, with local connectivity read as hydrogen valleys and inter-regional connectivity read as hydrogen corridors.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: It supplies an explicit, computable definition of 'valley' and 'corridor' that could replace the administrative boundaries currently used for designation.
insights.quote: We then quantify spatial spillover potential using network centrality measures, which capture connectivity between different offtakers.

insights.claim: The briefing situates its argument alongside work showing green hydrogen is a feasible abatement option primarily where electrification is technically or financially challenging, making the case for highly directed rather than broad policy support.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Green hydrogen's addressable market is deliberately framed as narrow, which is a constraint on any bullish hydrogen demand forecast.
insights.quote: This study argues that green hydrogen is a feasible abatement option primarily in sectors where electrification is technically or financially challenging, making the case for highly directed policy support.

insights.claim: Cited supporting literature cautions that energy technologies typically increase in unit size only after prolonged experimentation with smaller units, warning against policies that promote large-scale projects before a formative phase of learning.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: It is an implicit warning that giant flagship hydrogen projects may be premature, sitting in tension with the EU's gigawatt-scale ambitions.
insights.quote: energy technologies typically increase in unit size only after prolonged experimentation with smaller units, cautioning against policies that promote large-scale projects before a formative phase of learning

insights.claim: The work was produced by researchers at the Vienna University of Economics and Business, IIASA and the Complexity Science Hub, funded by the Austrian Federal Ministry for Innovation, Mobility and Infrastructure, with no competing interests declared.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
entities: Vienna University of Economics and Business
insights.so_what: The recommendations come from an Austrian public-funded academic group rather than an industry body, which is relevant to how EU policymakers will weigh them.
insights.quote: The contributions of C.R., B.Z. and K.S. were supported by the Austrian Federal Ministry for Innovation, Mobility and Infrastructure
